faq.a: Self-employment tax is the Social Security and Medicare tax paid by people who work for themselves. For 2026 it is 15.3% in total — 12.4% Social Security plus 2.9% Medicare — applied to 92.35% of your net self-employment earnings. Employees pay half through payroll and their employer pays the other half; self-employed people pay both halves.
Yes, if your net earnings from self-employment are $400 or more for the year, you owe self-employment tax. Below $400, no self-employment tax is due — though income tax rules still apply.
faq.q: Do I owe self-employment tax if my side hustle is small?

faq.a: The 12.4% Social Security part stops at the wage base: $184,500 for 2026 ($176,100 for 2025). The 2.9% Medicare part has no cap. An extra 0.9% Medicare tax can apply when self-employment income plus Medicare wages pass $200,000 single or $250,000 married filing jointly.
faq.q: Is there a cap on self-employment tax?

faq.a: One-half of your self-employment tax is deductible from your income tax. Federal income tax itself is separate from self-employment tax and depends on your total income and filing status — see the 2026 standard deduction and bracket figures in the note below.
faq.q: Can I deduct any of the self-employment tax?

whenNotToUse: This is an estimate of self-employment tax only — it does not calculate your federal or state income tax, which depend on your total income.
It does not handle the extra 0.9% Medicare tax in full (Form 8959) — it only flags when your income may pass the threshold.
It assumes all of your side-hustle income is self-employment income; rental, investment, and other income follow different rules.
